reviews.review: A great game if you love stalking people.

Written after completing episodes 1&2:

The Good:
Immersive, well put together and thought provoking. Orwell is a wonderful story based game that mimics reality in a believeable way.

The Bad:
Linear. I don't feel like I'm solving puzzles by scanning for information. I'm just following what's highlighted for me. It's a click based adventure first and a detective game second.

On balance though it's definitely worth playing.

The soundtrack is also quite nice and fits well with the game.

For those who love Big Brother conspiracy theories, this is a great game that allows you to participate in the Orwellian world from the other side. You are a member of a team that has access to a platform called Orwell that allows you to gather data on individuals. By piecing the information tidbits, called "datachunks", you get to understand various people's involvement in a certain incident.

Not only is the game mechanic fresh for me, the low-poly inspired graphics are very clean and good looking.

I'm just finished episode 2 and can't wait for episode 3, which is coming out on the 6th of November!

This game also gave me some stress symptoms: have to decide which place to pick, otherwise people will die. 
Can totally relate to the fictional situations in the game.


Absolutely worth the money.

A lot of people are praising this game, but it's really simple. There are very few choices with usually obvious consiquences.

Most of the game feels like work. You click and drag the things that are highlighted and then the guy reveals more plot points and gives you more documents to read while you click and drag more stuff. It's made all the more painful by false "upload" times (really? Uploading text to the most complex security system ever takes 3+ seconds each time!? Uploading that to Google Docs takes less time than that!) and phone and text conversations that play out in real time without any voice acting, so it mostly just feels like sitting and waiting for things to get done.

I understand people are interested in the story, or the greater point about surveillance, but as a game, this is just too simple. For a far better experience with a similar concept, I would highly suggest the ARG "This House Has People In It"

It's no coincidence that this game is released few days after I finished reading 1984...

In the game, it is not (yet?) the oppressed society of Oceania portrayed in 1984 but something much closer to today's headline of mass surveillance and data collection by intelligence agencies.  The game puts you in the role of an agent of the system and gives one a glimpse at the level of power of Orwell.  

The game doesn't make the investigation an obvious one.  One lead leads to a different lead and keeps one guessing.  One really has to analyze the data carefully.  What is and what is a smokescreen?  What is just an opinion vs. intent on action?

As many of the reviews state, it is not a long game (each episode is about an hour or so) but the merits of the game are quality over quantity.  

Big Brother is watching...

I began questioning myself. Safety and security is important, but at what cost? Is it ethical to comb through the private lives of these innocent people so I can point fingers at them and have them arrested as terrorists for the purpose of protecting "freedom"? Do my actions for the government violate the "freedom" that this claims to stand for? Am I tarnishing my own integrity, selling my soul for a paycheck? Can I look myself in the mirror every morning and tell myself I am doing what is necessary and right?

Then crucial conflicting evidence comes to light. I must make a rash decision. Lives are on the line. I must make a rash decision.
I make a decision.
I point a finger.
Men are sent into action to prevent bloodshed.
Did I make the right choice, or were my privacy invasions all for nothing?

I hold my breath.
Time presses on.

And then...
The news article is released. A tragedy averted. I saved lives. I made a difference.
I breathe a sigh of relief. I did it.
Can this really be wrong when it prevents mass genocide?
I have a duty to continue to exercise my power. To save lives. To protect the Nation and its citizens.
I reassure myself.
Sacrificing a little privacy for security is necessary to secure the freedoms of the people.
I am doing the right thing. What I must.
I will keep watching you.

I don't think I've ever had a game make me want to drop it and nnever come back quite like Orwell, not because it is bad, boring, or anything of the sort, but because of how well it succeeds in immersing you into the role of, well, pretty much 1984's Big brother.

The interesting, albeit not groundbreaking artstyle, simple and clean UI, and plethora of information for you to scroll through make for an interesting experience, but the real heavyweight for this game is no doubt its moral aspect.

Orwell makes you question your every decision, evrey snippet of information you submit seems to be able to screw up the life of an innocent person, or save people from death (and I hope future chapters continue to build on this). It makes you question the morality, ethics, and necessity of a government mass surveilance system, and shows you this from a new and unexpected point of view.

A unique idea executed well, but has a lack of content. What is there is excellent and I feel the price is probably reasonable for the ~4-6 hours of gameplay that we can expect from all 5 episodes (each episode has taken me well under an hour).

This game reflects many struggles relevant to the modern world: how much can we invade citizens' lives to potentially save others from terror attacks, how ethics are affected by the prevalent need of gathering intel, and finally, how what you do and post online can directly impact many lives. It's interesting to be put in charge of unraveling the web of events and linking them one to another. Another peculiar aspect is that there are two sides to the story and submitting wrong datachunks impacts further investigation. Taking all the fun bits of Watch Dogs/Papers Please and Her Story, Orwell paints the best kind of in-game surveillance experience to date, leaving me impatiently waiting for the next episode

The scariest game you can get before it becomes a horror title.

There's a story about a guy who wants revenge on his teacher, so he stalks through months of social meeds, finding alt emails and other accounts, until he finally finds a lead that wasn't buried if you just followed all the info through and has his revenge. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game about playing that guy, except with one or two extra powers: listening in on active conversations from people you've found, and looking through their computer if it's on and you have the serial number. With those two measly abilities you learn EVERYTHING about a half-dozen people and it's frightening finding out how much you find through the same fantasy Google that everyone else uses.

The game is also not all one side. Sure, its an invasion of privacy and a drastic abuse of power, but it works in teh end and the terrorists are caught.

Add in a dedication to making a believable universe and a neat artstyle and you have an interesting and engaging title, if flipping through people's Tumblr blogs, forum posts, and family history is your idea of fun.

Although tagged as "singleplayer" it's more fun if you have a friend or two over to 'watch' it with you and argue about who did/meant what as information is revealed, although that does slow things down.  Similarly, the more you read of the background and seemingly irrelevant information the more you learn about the world in which the story is set.  That also slows things down but means you get much more out of the game than simply 'solving' it.  The game also reacts well to irrelevant bits of information that you extract - I was told off for wasting time ^^.
All in all it's nicely put together and well worth the price.

Gotta say I took a risk and bought it based on the premise and what info you gather from the trailer alone. Did not disappoint. I must start with the "bad" - the game is episodic, and on release 2/5 "episodes" are available. Unfortunately, the game presents a focused story, so breaking off just as it starts to wind up is unpleasant. That said, the following episodes are supposed to be released within the upcoming three weeks, so I guess that's acceptable. 

On to the points.
[h1]Facts:[/h1] 
- [b]Point'n Read'n Click'n Drag gameplay[/b] - you read the articles, conversations, emails and based on the context decide which of the pre-selected information is important enough to send to the government for processing. When more info is found, more emails/sites/articles/conversations become available.

- [b]Limited game world[/b] - the game simulates a futuristic software that integrates spying application with a web browser. You'll be looking at articles, facebook walls and such for 95% of the game.

- [b]No voice over[/b] - all is text based

- [b]Ambient music[/b] - Music is toned down for the most part. It does pick up where necessary and serves as calming backdrop otherwise.

[h1]Good:[/h1]
- [b]Solid writing[/b]. The game focuses on creating a real, living world and the writing does the job well. All individual pieces are consistent with their role. The "facebook" walls look legit, news articles are written just as you'd expect them to be, chat/phone conversations are life-like as well.

- [b]Engrossing story[/b] While you can only experience 2/5th of it currently, it does a good job of setting the stage and presenting early high stakes challenge that you can succeed, but also fail at. I'm intrigued and want more asap.

- [b]Choices matter[/b] - nuff' said.


[h1]Bad:[/h1]
Nothing really stands out, the worst thing is episodic release. 

[h1]Suggestions[/h1]
- [b]More choices[/b] - I'd love to see the game a bit more complex, so that my experience is much different from my friends'.

While I like the concept, there's an arbitrary restriction that is frustratingly stupid and not justified within the scenario.  You're incapable of revising anything submitted, even when you receive better information later.  This problem is so obvious, even to the developers, that you will come across pieces of information that are marked as conflicting when you haven't yet received the information they conflict with.  In other cases, articles which would have helped you make the right choice are revealed right after you act on the incomplete information - not as the result of actions based on your old choice, mind you; you just haven't been drip-fed them yet.

6/10; poor implementation

In 2017, 6 years after the passing of the "Safety Bill" you are part of a new governmental domestic information taskforce that collects data on subjects and feeds them into the Orwell database. As the front-line of the information gathering, you select from highlighted bits which ones are correctly identified and which ones are superfluous, also resolving conflicted datapoints as required.

With its dystopian tone Orwell is a game about sleuthing, reading between the lines and - surprisingly - empathy. People often present a mixed online persona - some times we post out of anger, sometimes we change how we feel about each other, and often we say things that we later come to regret. We talk differently on our public blogs than we do with friends - which is the real persona? Does an angry post about "the government" mean they're a terrorist? Is this person actually a threat to the nation? Should I implicate their friends? Their co-workers? Their family?

Orwell is a worthy successor to games like "This War of Mine", "Cart Life" and "Papers, Please!" which challenge the action-packed nature of our AAA games for more emotional themes.

Before buying this game, I saw that most of the top rated reviews just spoke about comparison's to Orwellian works, modern social networks, and Papers Please. And I thought important to address a couple of things after playing through what is available. Orwell is an episodic game; meaning, this is not the final result. This is more of a "Whodunit" than a Thriller mystery, so judging it for linearity might be unfair since they attempt to make you the detective by providing you with a given set of aesthetics. Now talking about aesthetics, this game/experience has its obvious references to Orwell and "1984" -- mainly -- but it is very clear they are only used for inspiration. This is no de facto Orwell Fan Fiction, just an experienced based on some questions the devs had about resembling aspects of society. From the two episodes they have released, I can tell that this is comparable to Papers Please in that you have to provide an analysis to come up with game altering decisions. However, since this is a "Whodunit" type mystery, and are limited to less than half of the intended story arc, we cannot truly make that comparison. What I can say without spoiling, is that there are choices that can either save or spare hundreds of lives, and the deciding factor is actually a juxtaposition of logic I have yet to fully grasp and understand. I think this is a great game; yet, it remains an aesthetic experience we are not yet able to finalise. I look forward for Episode 3's release in three day's time.

Orwell plays its premise on its sleeve, but that's not a bad thing. Orwell's a lovely modern take on the dystopian Orwellian society from 1984, where surveillance is king and social media reveals your darkest secrets. The ruling government of your fictional country; rather menacingly known as, 'The Party'; is toned down to a believable level, less thought police coming to take those whom merely forget the government's new lie; more observing and taking people who know more than they think for a quick chat... In a windowless cell...

You play a new agent to an experimental scheme, brought about by their version of the patriot act, who spys on its people to counter terrorist acts. Unfortunately, you've come at a bad time, there's been a dramatic terrorist bombing and you've got to find those reponsible. Luckily, deus ex machina, you've been directed to a person of interest whom happens to be very weakly linked to the terrorist/s. Better start investigating. 

Investigations are done by exploring a person's current and past life in detail and it's a fun little bit of gameplay. You simply open either a website or a report and the, "government's advanced computers", scan the page for anything it thinks relevant to the investigation. It's up to you to decide what to include in your report by dragging and dropping highlighted items onto said report. Sadly, Osmotic Studios has decided that you can't change anything you drag onto your report. Accidentally mistake a bit of text saying they live in Wonderland as information on their mental instability rather than what the game has decided, which is that they physically live in Wonderland? Well tough titties, you can't change that. 

At times the game does spice things up with multiple choice moments. Throughout the game, contradictory information will be presented to you and it's up to you to decide which is the correct bit of information. But! But! There isn't always an obvious answer! Which infuriates a few people. But it shouldn't. People who get frustrated are sadly missing the obvious answer the game's trying to present to you. The truth doesn't matter. You are the truth. What you decide can and will be the truth. You pick the option which suits your needs, think person A is a dissdent to 'The Party'? Then the correct answer is that the man is a dissdent. No matter what contradictory information you see. This is the beauty of Orwell and this is were the game really shines. Sometimes though these options are forced. Two bits of information are in fact the same piece of information just it's presented in a way to force a choice, when in reality you could easily push both those pieces in a well worded report.

While the gameplay is enjoyable, where Orwell really shines is in it's narrative. The characters you are investigating are nicely fleshed out and you can get a real sense of who that person is and that's an important factor in a game like this. No matter how good a story you have, if the people you are investigating are dull or unbelievable it could really ruin a game like this, gladly I can say this hasn't happened. While it is rather short it has a nice progression and you can feel the underlying sense a deeper plot and the frustrating feeling of grasping at the strings of truth. A feeling further emphasised by the episodic nature of the game, gladly the timeframe is rather short and the feeling is rather than them having a product that isn't complete, they're trying to tailor the story from the fans suggestions and mood.

There weren't many things I disliked about Orwell. My biggest gripe is almost a personal choice, I've already mentioned a few smaller issues already such as forced choices and the fact information placed into the report cannot be edited, but I think Orwell misses a beat when it comes to power of the government. It wants to present a Orwellian society for the modern day and tries to do this by suggesting your powers and the government's powers are legally limited at certain moments. This is personally the opposite way I wish they had gone. For starters modern goverments have incredible powers just have a gander at the Patriot Act (US),  the 2000/2006 terrorism act (GB), and états d'urgence - constitution of 1958 (Fr). I wish Orwell had taken this and gone further, showing a government whose powers were even more unfettered.

In summation I rather like Orwell and it's a game I can very heartily recommend to anyone who would like a nice story driven narrative, and can get through the rather lengthy bits of text one has to read. There are some personal gripes I have with the story but overall nothing that you would really be a deal breaker.

If you like games where you are in control intelligence gathering as it pertains to a crime such as terrorism for example; this is a good game to purchase. While you are guided somewhat by a senior handler; you present your intelligence and data snippets to a central system for collection and retrieval purposes. You create the dots in many ways of an investigation and descern if the connections make sense or not. There will be conflicting information you have to decide if its credible or not. While game makes the information stand out for you to collect; you can turn off that setting and with that the game will become all the more difficult. Each episode so far has taken me roughly 90 min to do each. I read through the information throughly to understand the context that the highlight information is supporting. But if you just clicked though the information and saved the obvious; the game would not be an immersive experience. You will get what you put into it; and I think that factor is time and analyizing the information closely.
An interesting premise, gameplay that makes you think, and each episode is about an hour (the first is shorter). Well worth the price.

Orwell forces you to rethink the ideas of government, control, surveilance and the right to go : FK YOU; all presented inside the framework of the paranoid dystopian world originally created by George Orwell back in 1948.

Orwell, however is a modern, slick version of Oceania, in which you play a state agent gathering information on citizens in a world that is under perpetual surveilance.  Your role is to select relevant data bites to pass onto a computer system  designed to identify potential threats to the Nation's status quo. 

Where 1984 is a distant dystopia that can likened to far off places like North Korea,  the world of Orwell is far more like the very one we live in. Where the state operatus of Oceania is something that is menacing, power hungry and paranoid, the shades of powerplay in this world is deceptively bright, fresh and friendly, yet equally suspicious and potentially sinister. 

As you gather information you become acutely aware of your own actions and how they potentially affect the lives of the citizens you scrutinize, as you decide which bytes of information will be passed on and which will be hidden.  There are occasions where you will find contradictory information, presenting opposing beliefs, yet easily accepting the vailidy of both in your mind simultaneously.  However, unlike reading Orwell, and having the answers written out for you, here you are  co-conspirator in Big Brother. You start to question the ideas around good and  evil and discover things that potentially, are both.

The concept of the game is as fascinating as the mind games you start playing with yourself as you potentially prosecute or persecute citizens in a world where freedom and control are at constant odds with one another. 

There are more episodes to come,  and the final verdict will not be out for a while, but so far it is a unique and intriguing experience. Possibly the most rewarding asect about the game, is not the game itself, but the things you start to question, even when not playing the game. Though the brilliance of 1984 is in a league all by itself, there is no doubt that this games manages to bring the message in a far more suble way, and succeed in making it relevant to the world we live in today.

That in itself makes for unique and rewarding gameplay, and it would not be outrageous to suggest that Orwell breaks new ground  in the story/novel game genre.

On the flipside, the game is a little too easy, too much handholding and very linear, and the excecution, though good, could have been a lot better. 

HIghly recommended if you are an Orwell fan, even more so if you know little or nothing about 1984.

Hugely fun, and all at once very disturbing. Over the course of the first two episodes, I really didn't consider the ramifications. Yeah you're spying on people and the system you use is called "Orwell" but it doesn't sink in. At least not until the end.

I won't spoil anything, but the ending to Episode 2 is both the biggest argument for and against this type of surveillance. Because of you people will be saved or hurt, and the game never comes out and directly says it, but it's unlikely that any of it would have happened without the access you had. 

Orwell does more than provide yet another reason why privacy is important, it helps place you into the mindset of the people who thought up, made, and run these government programs and how in their minds, they're doing the right thing.  It makes you think, if only for a minute or two, and that's a pretty cool thing to do with only an hour and a bit to completion (so far, more episodes in November).

WHAT A GREAT GAME. Just finished the first two episodes and I am absolutely gripped by it. The third episode isn't out for another few days and I cannot wait to play more to uncover more of the mystery.

The best way I can describe it is a comparison to Hacknet - where that game is about hacking computers, Orwell is about hacking people's lives.

At first I was intrigeud by the concept of the game but after 30 minutes of gameplay it felt more like a guided tour than an interactive experience. 

The game starts with CCTV footage of a bombing at a plaza. In that footage a woman who has a criminal record is identified. From her you will start your investigation. The game presents you with newspaper articles, web pages as well as personal communication logs in which you will find marked passages of text or pictures, so called data junks, which you can upload to an agency to complete a person profile as well as finding connections to other people. 

Unfortunately you can't upload information which the game itself deems unrelevent. Some information which is rather useless needs to be uploaded to progress. Some information will even be taken out of context and there is nothing you can do than upload it and watch your handler making the wrong asumptions.

In one instance you have the profile of a person without the picture. You will find that persons picture very soon but will be unable to upload it. In another instance a data junk you can upload will be totally out of context from the conversation it can be taken. The worst was that on time where I could not upload proof of a direct connection beween a persons statement and the letter of intent which was sent to a ploice department prior to the bombing. Ironicly, at the very beginning, the game warns you to make sure not to upload anything that might be misleading or irellevant.

If you are looking for a story in wich you just press highlighted pieces of text to progress this might be the game for you. If you where hoping for a game in wich you are asked to find out what happened using online surveilance you might want to look somewhere else.

While the puzzle aspect is enjoyable, certain mechanics do result in feelings of repetitiveness and a lack of free exploration. More choices and information opportunities could be interesting, as well as perhaps a bit of tampering with the UI (everytime I use the Listener it feels like I have to wait two minutes for the computers to stop talking to each other just to click the datachunk, as it keeps moving down the page). Overall though, and especially as there have only been two episodes released, I have enjoyed this game enough to play each installment twice through, with different results, and still want to continue exploring the world Orwell allows us to explore: one of deceit, fear, and an underbelly of self-consiousness as you realize that you Big Brother.

This game is amazing.  While the first episode kind of takes you by the hand, the second one has you figuring out which data to use on your own. The further you progress in the game, the more you face the consequences of your previous choices. This game constantly has me feeling worried about the implications of my actions, which feel serious enough to have me clutching my pearls every now and then. I've waited impatiently for each episode to come out, and I've played through the game multiple times to see the difference my actions make. While the story is very linear, the endings and the characters reactions to events do vary, depending on your choices in the game.
I love the ethical dilemmas this game poses. After finishing an episode, I was left wanting more, but in the week long wait for the next episode I was also left wondering about how reflective this game is of current surveillance policies in place in various governments. It's an eerie feeling, and it's made me ponder my own activity online and how this would make me look in a similar system. 

TLDR: One of the most surprising, engrossing and entertaining games I've played in years. Hope another season or similar game is made by this team.
